items.title: 2026 Top AI Infrastructure Predictions — The Power Wall, The Compute Divide, and The Rise of Sovereign Stacks
items.summary: The problem with all the AI predictions for 2026 is not that they are wrong (or stating the obvious). It is that they assume AI progress will be a straight line. In reality, AI is entering a phase where choices about infrastructure will quietly decide outcomes. This is long before models ever reach users or their performance gets evaluated on benchmarks. These choices, whether enforced or by choice, now determine which projects get funded. Which products ship? Which regions and companies are allowed to scale? These decisions are already happening, and most of them have to do with algorithms and more to do with infrastructure. To understand how those decisions shape the year ahead, BigDATAwire reviewed and analyzed a large volume of AI infrastructure predictions for 2026. We looked for the deeper structural pressures that kept resurfacing across sources and grouped them into three core themes. For technology leaders and decision makers, these themes help clarify where AI investments are likely to pay off. It also shows the path where friction will emerge, and where expectations may need to be reset or at least managed. The Power Wall The power wall prediction is often viewed as a capacity challenge. And it is. However, it will increasingly act as a selection mechanism. This means that it will decide or even dictate what moves forward and what gets cut. It will separate the winners and the losers in terms of who has the right data and AI infrastructure to forge ahead. What this means at the product level, some AI features will never ship. They will be dropped early because they cost too much power at scale. At the company level, some organizations will scale AI while others fall behind. The difference will not necessarily be better models, but better access to power and infrastructure. At the geographical level, some regions will support advanced AI and others will not. Power limits and grid reliability will decide where AI can realistically run. In all such cases, the power wall acts as an important factor in decision-making. According to Oliver Steil, CEO at TeamViewer, “The AI energy crisis will force a fundamental reckoning across every industry – not just one sector or segment,” he says. “AI training and consumption will require more data centers, and the locations and energy sources of those data centers will come under intense scrutiny.” “Companies will hit an AI operations wall as projects scale from pilots to dozens of implementations. Technology and security leaders will face an AI operational bottleneck, struggling to scale from isolated pilots to enterprise-wide implementations.” (Shuttestock AI) In 2026, some AI workloads will not reach production at all. That’s an AI reality.  Of course, the reasons will differ by region and industry, but the pattern will be consistent. Power availability will constrain deployment in certain geographies. To make matters more challenging, carbon targets and public scrutiny will make large-scale AI rollouts politically difficult. Grid expansion will continue to lag demand. The result is a growing class of AI features that are delayed, downsized, or even quietly removed from product roadmaps before users ever encounter them. As AI systems move deeper into customer-facing services and core operations, the nature of failure changes as well. When infrastructure limits trigger outages or degraded performance, those incidents register as trust failures. They go beyond technical glitches. For organizations that position AI as a differentiator, reliability becomes inseparable from reputation. The power wall also plays a key role in how AI progress and success are measured. Model size and raw capability were hyped (and maybe overhyped). They are now starting to lose their status as primary indicators of AI sophistication or advancement. Efficiency is more important than ever now. We see metrics such as tokens per watt and cost per inference increasingly guide architectural and investment decisions. What this also means is a defensible moat for organizations that can deliver consistent AI outcomes within the ever-increasing physical and economic constraints around energy. That shift toward greater infrastructure efficiency is echoed by Sergio Gago, Chief Technology Officer at Cloudera. Kevin Roof, Director of Offer and Capture Management at LiquidStack, also expects that data center investors and operators will move beyond traditional efficiency measures in favor of a new one, arguing that “tokens per watt per dollar” will increasingly define success. He adds, “Since power constraints are the threshold preventing data center growth, organizations must use the power they have most effectively. Stranded power represents lost revenue.” What this ultimately changes is ambition. On stage and in press releases, autonomy still gets top billing. Inside organizations, the reality could be much different. The scope gets narrower. Fully autonomous designs quietly turn into assistive systems. Humans stay in the loop longer than originally planned. And all this won’t be necessarily because the technology cannot handle more, but because running autonomy at scale starts to look expensive and risky. In 2026, the power wall will not just slow AI down, but it will also dictate what actually gets built, what gets scaled back, and what never makes it out of planning at all. The Compute Divide At BigDATAwire, we have covered how compute divide is creating tension in the AI and data world. Reading through 2026 AI infrastructure predictions, we saw a lot on compute divide. We can be certain that access to compute is no longer assumed. It is increasingly earned, negotiated, or, in some cases, just quietly denied. On paper, cloud was supposed to level the field. However, in practice, it is doing the opposite. High-end GPU access is becoming uneven and unpredictable. It is also becoming expensive at exactly the moment when demand is exploding. While some organizations can lock in capacity years in advance, others are left refreshing dashboards and watching quotas tighten. This is forcing them to adjust their plans based on whatever compute happens to be available during the month or quarter. This is not a temporary supply hiccup. It shows up repeatedly across predictions this year. Enterprises with capital and long planning horizons are securing dedicated capacity, whether through private AI environments, long-term hyperscaler agreements, or emerging neocloud providers built around guaranteed access. (Krot_Studio/Shutterstock) Smaller teams and startups increasingly operate on shared infrastructure where performance fluctuates and pricing changes without much warning. That difference matters more than most AI narratives admit. What changes first is behavior. Teams with stable compute access design ambitious systems. They are not worried about compute resources. They have a higher margin for errors. They can tolerate some failure. Teams without it become cautious. Roadmaps narrow. Use cases get trimmed. Over time, those choices compound, and the gap widens. Not because of talent or ideas, but because of infrastructure certainty. Even in regions where energy is available, advanced compute clusters tend to form around cloud regions and mature data center ecosystems. Some places become builders and operators of AI systems. Others become consumers by default. The distinction is rarely framed this way, but it shows up clearly in deployment patterns. Efficiency adds another layer. Several predictions point to a growing advantage for organizations that know how to use compute well. Not just acquire it, but orchestrate it, schedule it, and squeeze value out of every cycle. For some, the hardware may even be available, but it is poorly utilized. That is the compute divide. The Rise of Sovereign Stacks The rise of sovereign stacks marks the end of a convenient illusion that has shaped AI thinking for most of the last decade. That illusion is that cloud would abstract away ownership, location, and even jurisdiction. That AI could run anywhere. It could scale endlessly. And remain largely indifferent to borders, regulators, or infrastructure politics. Well, the 2026 predictions we analyzed tell a different story. Control is now at the center of AI strategy. It is now an operational requirement. It brings back some of the above-mentioned factors that cloud was built to overcome. Now, enterprises are not optimizing purely for speed or model capability; they are optimizing for where systems run and how exposed they are to forces they do not control. Several predictions point to the growing importance of private AI and on-premises infrastructure. So is the cloud dead? No, not at all. However, as a response to growing concentration and dependency, enterprises are looking for ways to regain leverage over their data. And as a result have more control over their workloads and cost structures. Private AI factories and on-prem systems are projected to reclaim a meaningful share because they offer something that shared infrastructure increasingly cannot. Predictability. (Shutterstock AI Image) Sovereignty also emerges as a practical constraint. Multiple predictions highlight how privacy and regulation are shaping where AI workloads can realistically be deployed. These pressures influence cloud investment decisions, data center placement, and even architectural choices. The assumption that AI can simply run wherever capacity is cheapest no longer holds. What accelerates this shift is the rise of autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents. Era of Agentic AI. The predictions warn that existing governance models are ill-equipped to manage fleets of short-lived agents acting across systems at machine speed. In response, organizations are seeking tighter control planes, shared standards, and infrastructure they can audit end-to-end. Sovereignty begins to extend beyond data into algorithms and execution layers. The result is fragmentation. Not a desirable for any organization. AI workloads are increasingly optimized for compliance, reliability, and jurisdictional certainty, not just global scale. Hybrid architectures stop being transitional and become permanent. Sovereign stacks emerge as layered systems where compute and data are intentionally anchored. If you want to read more stories like this and stay ahead of the curve in data, AI, and infrastructure, subscribe to BigDataWire and follow us on LinkedIn . We deliver the insights, reporting, and breakthroughs that define the next era of technology. items.summary_html:
The problem with all the AI predictions for 2026 is not that they are wrong (or stating the obvious). It is that they assume AI progress will be a straight line. In reality, AI is entering a phase where choices about infrastructure will quietly decide outcomes. This is long before models ever reach users or their performance gets evaluated on benchmarks. These choices, whether enforced or by choice, now determine which projects get funded. Which products ship? Which regions and companies are allowed to scale? These decisions are already happening, and most of them have to do with algorithms and more to do with infrastructure. 

To understand how those decisions shape the year ahead, BigDATAwire reviewed and analyzed a large volume of AI infrastructure predictions for 2026. We looked for the deeper structural pressures that kept resurfacing across sources and grouped them into three core themes. For technology leaders and decision makers, these themes help clarify where AI investments are likely to pay off. It also shows the path where friction will emerge, and where expectations may need to be reset or at least managed.  

The Power Wall

The power wall prediction is often viewed as a capacity challenge. And it is. However, it will increasingly act as a selection mechanism. This means that it will decide or even dictate what moves forward and what gets cut. It will separate the winners and the losers in terms of who has the right data and AI infrastructure to forge ahead. 

What this means at the product level, some AI features will never ship. They will be dropped early because they cost too much power at scale. At the company level, some organizations will scale AI while others fall behind. The difference will not necessarily be better models, but better access to power and infrastructure. At the geographical level, some regions will support advanced AI and others will not. Power limits and grid reliability will decide where AI can realistically run. In all such cases, the power wall acts as an important factor in decision-making. 

According to Oliver Steil, CEO at TeamViewer, “The AI energy crisis will force a fundamental reckoning across every industry – not just one sector or segment,” he says. “AI training and consumption will require more data centers, and the locations and energy sources of those data centers will come under intense scrutiny.”

“Companies will hit an AI operations wall as projects scale from pilots to dozens of implementations. Technology and security leaders will face an AI operational bottleneck, struggling to scale from isolated pilots to enterprise-wide implementations.”

                          (Shuttestock AI)

In 2026, some AI workloads will not reach production at all. That’s an AI reality.  Of course, the reasons will differ by region and industry, but the pattern will be consistent. Power availability will constrain deployment in certain geographies. To make matters more challenging, carbon targets and public scrutiny will make large-scale AI rollouts politically difficult. Grid expansion will continue to lag demand. The result is a growing class of AI features that are delayed, downsized, or even quietly removed from product roadmaps before users ever encounter them.

As AI systems move deeper into customer-facing services and core operations, the nature of failure changes as well. When infrastructure limits trigger outages or degraded performance, those incidents register as trust failures. They go beyond technical glitches. For organizations that position AI as a differentiator, reliability becomes inseparable from reputation. 

The power wall also plays a key role in how AI progress and success are measured. Model size and raw capability were hyped (and maybe overhyped). They are now starting to lose their status as primary indicators of AI sophistication or advancement. 

Efficiency is more important than ever now. We see metrics such as tokens per watt and cost per inference increasingly guide architectural and investment decisions. What this also means is a defensible moat for organizations that can deliver consistent AI outcomes within the ever-increasing physical and economic constraints around energy.

That shift toward greater infrastructure efficiency is echoed by Sergio Gago, Chief Technology Officer at Cloudera. 

Kevin Roof, Director of Offer and Capture Management at LiquidStack, also expects that data center investors and operators will move beyond traditional efficiency measures in favor of a new one, arguing that “tokens per watt per dollar” will increasingly define success. He adds, “Since power constraints are the threshold preventing data center growth, organizations must use the power they have most effectively. Stranded power represents lost revenue.”

What this ultimately changes is ambition. On stage and in press releases, autonomy still gets top billing. Inside organizations, the reality could be much different. The scope gets narrower. Fully autonomous designs quietly turn into assistive systems. Humans stay in the loop longer than originally planned. And all this won’t be necessarily because the technology cannot handle more, but because running autonomy at scale starts to look expensive and risky. 

In 2026, the power wall will not just slow AI down, but it will also dictate what actually gets built, what gets scaled back, and what never makes it out of planning at all.

The Compute Divide

At BigDATAwire, we have covered how compute divide is creating tension in the AI and data world. Reading through 2026 AI infrastructure predictions, we saw a lot on compute divide. We can be certain that access to compute is no longer assumed. It is increasingly earned, negotiated, or, in some cases, just quietly denied.

On paper, cloud was supposed to level the field. However, in practice, it is doing the opposite. High-end GPU access is becoming uneven and unpredictable. It is also becoming expensive at exactly the moment when demand is exploding. While some organizations can lock in capacity years in advance, others are left refreshing dashboards and watching quotas tighten. This is forcing them to adjust their plans based on whatever compute happens to be available during the month or quarter.

This is not a temporary supply hiccup. It shows up repeatedly across predictions this year. Enterprises with capital and long planning horizons are securing dedicated capacity, whether through private AI environments, long-term hyperscaler agreements, or emerging neocloud providers built around guaranteed access. 

                (Krot_Studio/Shutterstock)

Smaller teams and startups increasingly operate on shared infrastructure where performance fluctuates and pricing changes without much warning. 

That difference matters more than most AI narratives admit.

What changes first is behavior. Teams with stable compute access design ambitious systems. They are not worried about compute resources. They have a higher margin for errors. They can tolerate some failure. Teams without it become cautious. Roadmaps narrow. Use cases get trimmed. Over time, those choices compound, and the gap widens. Not because of talent or ideas, but because of infrastructure certainty.

Even in regions where energy is available, advanced compute clusters tend to form around cloud regions and mature data center ecosystems. Some places become builders and operators of AI systems. Others become consumers by default. The distinction is rarely framed this way, but it shows up clearly in deployment patterns.

Efficiency adds another layer. Several predictions point to a growing advantage for organizations that know how to use compute well. Not just acquire it, but orchestrate it, schedule it, and squeeze value out of every cycle. For some, the hardware may even be available, but it is poorly utilized. That is the compute divide. 

The Rise of Sovereign Stacks

The rise of sovereign stacks marks the end of a convenient illusion that has shaped AI thinking for most of the last decade. That illusion is that cloud would abstract away ownership, location, and even jurisdiction. That AI could run anywhere. It could scale endlessly. And remain largely indifferent to borders, regulators, or infrastructure politics. Well, the 2026 predictions we analyzed tell a different story.

Control is now at the center of AI strategy. It is now an operational requirement. It brings back some of the above-mentioned factors that cloud was built to overcome. Now, enterprises are not optimizing purely for speed or model capability; they are optimizing for where systems run and how exposed they are to forces they do not control.

Several predictions point to the growing importance of private AI and on-premises infrastructure. So is the cloud dead? No, not at all. However, as a response to growing concentration and dependency, enterprises are looking for ways to regain leverage over their data. And as a result have more control over their workloads and cost structures. Private AI factories and on-prem systems are projected to reclaim a meaningful share because they offer something that shared infrastructure increasingly cannot. Predictability.

                 (Shutterstock AI Image) 

Sovereignty also emerges as a practical constraint. Multiple predictions highlight how privacy and regulation are shaping where AI workloads can realistically be deployed. These pressures influence cloud investment decisions, data center placement, and even architectural choices. The assumption that AI can simply run wherever capacity is cheapest no longer holds.

What accelerates this shift is the rise of autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents. Era of Agentic AI. The predictions warn that existing governance models are ill-equipped to manage fleets of short-lived agents acting across systems at machine speed. 

In response, organizations are seeking tighter control planes, shared standards, and infrastructure they can audit end-to-end. Sovereignty begins to extend beyond data into algorithms and execution layers.

The result is fragmentation. Not a desirable for any organization. AI workloads are increasingly optimized for compliance, reliability, and jurisdictional certainty, not just global scale. Hybrid architectures stop being transitional and become permanent. Sovereign stacks emerge as layered systems where compute and data are intentionally anchored.

items.title: Impact of the EU Data Act on Cloud Services
items.summary: As part of the EU’s data strategy, Regulation on Harmonized Rules on Fair Access and Use of Data ( Data Act ) became applicable on September 12th, 2025. The Data Act aims to create a fairer data market in which customers gain more control over their data and can switch easily between service providers. For cloud service providers (CSPs) this means new contractual, transparency and governance obligations. Key obligations for CSPs 1. Switching between data processing services The Data Act obliges CSPs to remove all pre-commercial, commercial, technical, contractual, or organizational barriers that might prevent customers from switching to another service provider or to an on-premise solution. In practice, the contractual terms governing the use of cloud services must allow switching and clearly describe the switching process. CSPs must also publish the technical information needed for data portability on their website and provide support for customers during the transition period. 2. Egress fees To further support switching, the Data Act prohibits all switching charges, including data egress fees, effective from January 12th, 2027. Until that date, any charges imposed by CSPs for switching must be transparently disclosed in the contract and may not exceed the costs “directly linked” to the switching process. 3. International governmental access and transfer Complementing the existing rules on data transfers under the GDPR, Chapter VII of the Data Act introduces rules for international governmental access and transfer of non-personal data . In practice, CSPs must include transparent information on their websites about the jurisdiction their infrastructure is subject to and the concrete safeguards it has implemented to prevent unlawful international governmental access to the data they process. UpCloud’s compliance with the EU Data Act UpCloud’s services are designed with interoperability and customer autonomy at the core. Customers retain the freedom to port their data and switch to another provider at any time through our APIs. Should the customer prefer to initiate a formal switching procedure, UpCloud’s Terms of Service set out a framework for the transition, under which UpCloud will support customers’ exit plans and ensure business continuity and data security. With zero-cost egress , there are concerns over transfer fees. UpCloud maintains a strict stance on international governmental access requests to data. We do not disclose any data to governmental authorities except where required under the laws of Finland. All requests from foreign authorities are redirected to the appropriate Finnish authorities in accordance with national law and established mutual legal assistance frameworks. This ensures that any possible disclosure is done lawfully and subject to proper judicial oversight. Further details regarding jurisdiction and about our measures to prevent international governmental access can be found here . For additional  questions, contact our team.

As part of the EU’s data strategy, Regulation on Harmonized Rules on Fair Access and Use of Data (Data Act ) became applicable on September 12th, 2025. 

The Data Act aims to create a fairer data market in which customers gain more control over their data and can switch easily between service providers. For cloud service providers (CSPs) this means new contractual, transparency and governance obligations. 

Key obligations for CSPs

1. Switching between data processing services

The Data Act obliges CSPs to remove all pre-commercial, commercial, technical, contractual, or organizational barriers that might prevent customers from switching to another service provider or to an on-premise solution. 

In practice, the contractual terms governing the use of cloud services must allow switching and clearly describe the switching process. CSPs must also publish the technical information needed for data portability on their website and provide support for customers during the transition period. 

2. Egress fees

To further support switching, the Data Act prohibits all switching charges, including data egress fees, effective from January 12th, 2027. Until that date, any charges imposed by CSPs for switching must be transparently disclosed in the contract and may not exceed the costs “directly linked” to the switching process.

3. International governmental access and transfer

Complementing the existing rules on data transfers under the GDPR, Chapter VII of the Data Act introduces rules for international governmental access and transfer of non-personal data. In practice, CSPs must include transparent information on their websites about the jurisdiction their infrastructure is subject to and the concrete safeguards it has implemented to prevent unlawful international governmental access to the data they process.

UpCloud’s compliance with the EU Data Act

UpCloud’s services are designed with interoperability and customer autonomy at the core. 

Customers retain the freedom to port their data and switch to another provider at any time through our APIs. Should the customer prefer to initiate a formal switching procedure, UpCloud’s Terms of Service set out a framework for the transition, under which UpCloud will support customers’ exit plans and ensure business continuity and data security. With zero-cost egress, there are concerns over transfer fees.

UpCloud maintains a strict stance on international governmental access requests to data. We do not disclose any data to governmental authorities except where required under the laws of Finland. All requests from foreign authorities are redirected to the appropriate Finnish authorities in accordance with national law and established mutual legal assistance frameworks. This ensures that any possible disclosure is done lawfully and subject to proper judicial oversight.

Further details regarding jurisdiction and about our measures to prevent international governmental access can be found here. For additional  questions, contact our team.

items.title: Top 5 enterprise tech priorities for 2026
items.summary: It’s the season for “looking ahead to next year” articles that tell some group or another what they should be doing or what some “expert” says they should do. Let’s take a different slant and focus on what one group— arguably the most important tech buyer group — actually says they’re going to do. I’ve collected 284 comments on tech priorities for 2026 from enterprises, and here are the top five. 1. AI optimization and uncertainty Let’s start with a priority that embraces two unsurprising sentiments. The first is that the top priority, cited by 211 of the enterprises, is to “deploy the hardware, software, data, and network tools needed to optimize AI project value.” The second is that there is significant uncertainty regarding just what those tools are and even over whether they could be confidently identified. The great majority of the 211 said that their focus is on the agent form of AI, but recall from this blog that enterprises have always seen three distinct agent models: the “interactive” one workers used much like we use chatbot AI today, the “workflow” model that sits in an application workflow like another piece of software, and the “embedded” form that’s built into an application. Enterprises think they have a handle on workflow AI, in terms of what it runs on and what it connects to. But even there, many enterprises say that a new AI element in the workflow is useful because it integrates insights drawn from a broader set of sources, which might in theory be anywhere, data-wise. And they’re even less sure about the impact of the other two models. Embedded AI agents are mostly used in either business analytics or to support network or IT operations, and both these missions seem to put AI in a simple extension role, so aren’t generally expected to require a lot of rethinking on infrastructure or practices. Not so, say enterprises. AI agents are, in general, data magnets. They want more information, they want more consistent information, and they need some measure of data value or weight in making decisions. For example, a netops AI tool might want information on seasonal sales patterns to forecast traffic better. Without broader information sources, it’s harder to build enough value to make a business case, and AI use of data is often implicit in how the model works, where traditional applications use data because the developer called for it. How do you know what AI is going to call for? The interactive form of AI poses the greatest risk. While enterprises see this model as limited to perhaps ten or fifteen percent of workers, those with the highest unit value of labor, it’s nearly impossible to predict what resources a given worker interaction might demand. “One question could use as much compute, as much data, and generate as much traffic, as a week’s running of a normal application,” one planner complained, noting that this sudden resource draw-down can actually impact IT performance across a big chunk of the business. And interactive agents might broad access permission, raising data governance concerns. Enterprises agree you never want to give an agent access to everything. First, obviously, this would create massive privacy and governance risks, but second, there’s a significant risk generated by any sort of redundancy in the data. It does beyond simple deduplication, too. Enterprises recommend against using a mixture of detail and summary data, including “derived” data. There’s a risk that working on mixed detail levels can bias results accidentally. “Twenty summaries of the same detail data can look to AI like twenty other sources,” one enterprise noted. IBM’s decision to buy Confluent , a known player in building data-flow applications, may be linked to the data access control and governance issue. 2. Cloud backups The second priority is also unsurprising given recent news. Of 284 enterprises who commented, 173 said that they needed a strategy to back up cloud components in the event of cloud outages . This, they say, is a lot more complicated than senior management thinks. First, you have to decide just what really needs backed up. “You can’t totally immunize yourself against a massive cloud or Internet problem,” say planners. Most cloud outages, they note, resolve in a maximum of a few hours, so you can let some applications ride things out. When you know the “what,” you can look at the “how.” Is multi-cloud the best approach, or can you build out some capacity in the data center? Enterprises note that building in resilience in any form may require redesigning some applications to make cloud-hosted elements portable, and that can also mean looking at where application data is stored and how access to it is connected. 3. Infrastructure simplification Priority three is managing the technical complexity of infrastructure, cited by 139 enterprises. “We have too many things to buy and to manage,” one planner said. “Too many sources, too many technologies.” Nobody thinks they can do some massive fork-lift restructuring (there’s no budget), but they do believe that current projects can be aligned to a long-term simplification strategy. This, interestingly, is seen by over a hundred of the group as reducing the number of vendors. They think that “lock-in” is a small price to pay for greater efficiency and reduction in operations complexity, integration, and fault isolation. This is the biggest shift against multi-vendor or open infrastructure I’ve ever seen. 4. Prioritize governance The close number four priority is more administrative than infrastructure-related; 124 enterprises in our group said they needed to “totally revamp governance.” Yes, AI is a big factor in this, but so is the elastic-hosting model of cloud and multi-cloud, and the “sovereignty” issues associated with operating across multiple jurisdictions, and the increasingly chaotic nature of regulations. The percentage of enterprises who say they need some formal “government affairs” input to management practices has increased from 12% in 2020 to 47% for 2026. For example, EU cloud and AI sovereignty concerns impact plans for both AI and cloud application resilience. The biggest problem, these enterprises say, is that governance has tended to be applied to projects at the planning level, meaning that absent major projects, governance tended to limp along based on aging reviews. Enterprises note that, like AI, orderly expansions in how applications and data are used can introduce governance issues, just like changes in laws and regulations. AI complicates this because it’s difficult or impossible to know just what data AI is accessing, if there are no filters on data availability. All this is a governance challenge, but it can pale in comparison to the fact that companies aren’t used to even thinking about governance absent a project framework. Do you need to create “governance projects?” If so, how are they justified, funded? Where there are hard changes in law or regulations, there are procedures, but not so much with other challenges. AI agents, even workflow agents, can creep into governance problems as usage grows, for example. 5. Cost management The final priority on our list, with 108 enterprises citing it, is in many ways a barrier to fulfilling any of the other goals they identify: Do more for less. Of our 284 enterprises, 226 said that they were under more budget pressure for 2026, and only 9 said they had less pressure (for the rest, pressures were the same). It’s interesting, though, that number five on the priorities list is the lowest scored for cost management since 2008/2009. The interesting thing about this particular priority is that, unlike prior years where the “cost” being managed was presumed to be the capital cost of the technologies involved, the equipment and software, the focus for 2026 is the total cost, what would be classified as “total cost of ownership” or TCO. This would be easy, or at least possible, in the context of traditional project thinking, but so many of these priorities blur the lines between “projects” that require review, justification, and approval, and normal day-to-day business decisions that usually dodge much of that formality. How do you assess the TCO of AI efficiency optimization overall, or cloud application resilience, or governance​? Overall, the comments from enterprises suggest that while they’re prioritizing many expected issues, they’re also dealing with more subtle ones, and even on topics like AI, they’re taking a different slant than many had expected. It’s more about their ecosystem than the individual parts, and that should make 2026 an interesting year with a lot of important trends to watch!

items.title: IBM Research Introduces CUGA, an Open-Source Configurable Agent Framework on Hugging Face
items.summary: IBM Research has released CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) on Hugging Face Spaces, making its enterprise-oriented agent framework easier to evaluate with open models and real workflows. The move positions CUGA as a practical alternative to brittle, tightly coupled agent frameworks that often struggle with tool misuse, long-horizon reasoning, and recovery from failure. By Robert Krzaczyński
